line: But they only got two more years of slavery to do harm to us
vault_lines: But they only got two more years of slavery to do harm to us
meaning:
Kodak has previously approached the idea that slavery still exists nowadays—despite its official abolition with the 13th Amendment in 1865—in a June 2017 tweet.

Kodak, who is known for being a spiritual person, refers to the Bible and alludes to Acts 7:6, in which God said to Abram:

Your descendants will be strangers in a foreign land, where they will be in slavery and oppressed for four hundred years.

Following Kodak’s reasoning, 1619 being the date when slavery started, 2019 would mark the end of the 400-years bondage described by God in Acts 7:6.

line: This can’t be, “Land of the free” If kneeling might cost your position
vault_lines: This can't be, "Land of the free"
meaning:
Dreezy is referring to the U.S. national anthem protests.
In 2016, American athletes started kneeling during the national anthem. The act itself expresses their rage against police brutality towards the black community.
The instigator of the movement was San Francisco 49ers quarterback, Colin Kaepernick who kneeled during the anthem and encouraged many other NFL players to do the same.



 Colin Kaepernick and Eric Reid kneeling during the national anthem prior to the 49ers' season opener. 

In September 2017, the movement went further when players protested against Donald Trump.
Trump’s response to the players who knelt to the anthem was:
“Maybe you shouldn’t be in the country.” 
He also lauded the NFL’s new guidelines in which, from now on, kneeling is prohibited.
https://twitter.com/foxandfriends/status/999599639996313600
Since then, any violation of this specific rule will cost the player his position.

The artist is, therefore questioning the logic behind this specific NFL rule: how can the United States be a free country when the act of kneeling on the field will get you fired?

Granny still scratching lottos up,” 'cause that’s real shit.

line: Man, take our culture, our blueprint Pay the knockoff to come model us
vault_lines: Man, take our culture, our blueprint
meaning:
It’s just too many times that I see trends from our people that get bashed, get called ratchet, “You can’t come to work like this.” “You’ll never get a job like this.” “You’re hair is nappy.” You know, just a lot of things that people say, and then later you’ll see it be in fashion and all of these things in magazines and stuff. But I just feel like my people’s just so creative. Every race, everybody has what’s special about them, what they’re good at, and I feel like we all can be equal in one way, but I just feel like we uniquely have a certain aura about ourselves. We have a certain type of creativity and it’s different from everybody else.

Just like Chinese creativity and art is different from ours, and we like to look at their stuff and influence. And even Caucasian has their own artistic ways. And we look at their fashion, you know, high-end and however way they do it. I feel like ours usually gets dismissed, and then it comes back up and it makes millions for whoever wants to capitalize off of it. And that’s bogus. We need to start hiring some of these people that’s coming up with the things in our culture to be creative directors and push the culture forward. You feel me? Like, we just need more jobs for what we’re doing. They look at our stuff, even when I got pulled over the other day, what I was telling you about, the lady that was trying to get me with the weed. I’m just like, “I ain’t got no weed on me,” she like, “Why you smell like weed?” I was like, “‘Cause I was at the studio. I do music.” “Oh, well that’s what you get for being with the rappers, doing with the…”

It’s just like, damn this a whole job. I was like, damn that’s what I get for rapping? But that’s just how it is. People look at what we do like it’s crazy, or like it’s just a hustle or like we just trying to get on or something. And it’s like, nah, this how I feed my family. I go work from 9 to 9, or I’m in the studio for 12 hours straight. Going in my passion, my art, but people don’t take that as serious.

line: My word is bond as fuck
vault_lines: My word is bond as fuck
meaning:
This line references both the more recent YG 2016 song “Word is Bond,” but also the phrases’s long-standing role in hip hop as a statement of the importance of the spoken word as well as the authenticity of the message being conveyed in the music.

As recounted in “The Origins of the Phrase ‘Word is Bond,’”

As most of the best emcees at the time [the ‘80s] began using “word is bond” (including LL Cool J), the phrase entered into the public consciousness as a hip-hop term. Although not everybody understood it’s meaning, it would become more recognisable with each passing year.

Dreezy’s use is consistent with this longer history; it means that in her raps, she is speaking absolutely nothing but the truth, without exaggeration.

line: Look my word is bond as fuck My life is hard enough They not rewarding us They disregarding us And if I go to D.C., I’m tryna spar with Trump I’m not a politician, just can’t ignore the stuff
vault_lines: And if I go to D.C., I'm tryna spar with Trump
meaning:
6LACK speaks on black lives in this chorus. Recently elected President Donald Trump has not been entirely in support of the blacks in the United States in recent days.

The National Anthem Issue, an issue that has enveloped the sports world, involves many African American football players either kneeling, holding up a fist, or in some cases, not even coming out of the locker room during the playing of the national anthem. This started when former 49ers quarterback  Colin Kaepernick kneeled during the playing of the national Anthem.

Colin said:

I am not going to stand up to show pride in a flag for a country that oppresses black people and people of color. To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way. There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder

As more and more players stood up for black rights. Donald Trump took matters into his own hands. He tweeted:

If NFL fans refuse to go to games until players stop disrespecting our Flag & Country, you will see change take place fast. Fire or suspend!

This shocked the American community, and some people responded. Eminem’s freestyle on the BET awards is a great example of this. 6LACK is saying that if he ever goes to Washington D.C., Capital of the United States and home of Donald Trump, he wants to stand up for black rights and spar with the president. 6LACK follows this up by saying that even though he doesn’t usually get into politics, he can’t ignore the actions President Trump is taking.

line: These people got weather control Where the hell you think Hurricane Harvey from?

meaning:
HAARP is a governmental run program to control weather, which Kodak is referring to in this line. This program is used for cloud seeding to stabilize the change in the atmosphere due to global warming.

But in this verse Kodak is stating that they are using that same program to create “natural disaster” storms to push out all minorities in the city as it is becoming more popular to live in the city… gentrification.
